methods.notes: Rebadged TTLock deadbolts commonly advertise an "S2xx"-style name whose suffix is the reversed last-6-MAC. Because OEMs rename freely, confirm by connecting and exchanging a 7F 5A-framed packet.

manufacturer_data.description:
The BLE advertisement local name encodes the last 6 MAC octets in REVERSED byte order (e.g. a name ending "_abcdef" corresponds to MAC ...ef:cd:ab). Many rebadged models advertise an "S2xx" style name.
Manufacturer data carries lock state, so status can be tracked passively with no connection (reported, roquerodrigo/ha-ttlock-ble): protocol type, sub-version and scene (the first three frame-header values), the bolt position and battery level, an indication that unsynced operation-log records are waiting, and the lock's own MAC, which that integration checks against the advertiser address before trusting a payload. A dormant lock advertises without a usable bolt position (battery only). The lock stops advertising while a session is held open. The byte offsets live in that project's separate ttlock-ble SDK and are not recorded here yet. Its Bluetooth matcher keys on manufacturer ID 773 (0x0305); hypothesis, not checked: that is not a SIG company assignment but protocol type 5 / sub-version 3 sitting in the company-ID slot (05 03 on the wire), so it would miss locks on other protocol versions -- do not use it as a sole matcher.

device.manufacturer: Sciener (TTLock platform) — rebadged by hundreds of OEMs
device.name: TTLock / Sciener BLE Locks (rebadged smart deadbolts, padlocks, cabinet locks)
device.notes:
TTLock is a white-label BLE lock stack by Sciener, rebadged by a huge number of OEMs (generic "S2xx" smart deadbolts, padlocks, cabinet locks). Sciener is active and ships a closed Android/iOS SDK and a cloud, but does NOT publish the BLE wire protocol; the community has partially reverse-engineered it. Local control is possible: the cloud is only for key/passcode issuance, and once a client holds the lock's per-lock credential set it can lock and unlock over BLE offline. That set is more than the AES key (reported, from roquerodrigo/ha-ttlock-ble's account-free manual-key path): the lock MAC, the 16-byte AES key, the numeric unlock key (as issued at initialisation, not the obfuscated form the vendor cloud returns), an optional numeric admin passcode, and the five frame-header values below. Lock/unlock needs no admin passcode, but passcode management and the sound setting do, and a hand-entered key often lacks it -- so basic actuation working is not proof that admin features will. The cloud's other per-key fields (user id, validity window) never reach the wire: that integration sends its user-time check with a zeroed user id and the firmware's permanent-key date values. The same integration offers Schlage Breeze accounts as a second TTLock-platform app at sign-in; that does not establish that every Breeze lock works on the manual-key path.
GATT: command writes on characteristic 0000fff2 (write-without-response), status notifications on 0000fff4; battery is the standard 0x2A19 under 0x180F. (A Nordic legacy DFU service 00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 is also present for OTA. Only its presence is recorded, in features[type: firmware_update], so a generic client knows to keep out of it; the update procedure is deliberately not documented: bricking risk.)
FRAME: [12-byte header][16-32 byte data][3-byte tail]. Header bytes 0-1 are the fixed magic 7F 5A; byte 2 protocol type, byte 3 sub-version, byte 4 scene, bytes 5-6 groupId, bytes 7-8 orgId, byte 9 command id, byte 10 encryption flag, byte 11 data length. Tail = 1 byte CRC-8/MAXIM over header+payload, then CRLF (0D 0A) terminating every packet. The header values are per lock: ha-ttlock-ble defaults to protocol type 5, sub-version 3, scene 2, groupId 1, orgId 1 and describes those as right for most V3 locks, not for every TTLock variant (reported). The lock advertises its own protocol type, sub-version and scene, so a client can read those three from a scan and check them before connecting; a wrong value shows up as a lock that never answers.
CRYPTO: data is AES/CBC/PKCS5, 16-byte blocks, with the IV equal to the key (16 bytes). A pre-AES XOR obfuscation is applied per byte using a 256-entry CRC table. Encryption is confirmed for protocol 5 / sub-version 3; the AES key (aesKeyArray) is retrieved from the lock after successful pairing (it is NOT one global constant). Auth is a custom multi-packet key exchange, not standard BLE bonding.

openness.notes: Sciener publishes a closed SDK (black-box native lock core) and a registered-developer cloud API, but not the BLE frame/crypto. The community RE is the only open wire documentation and is incomplete (the AES key-exchange is not fully solved).

upstream_docs.covers: The GATT UUIDs, the 7F 5A frame layout, CRC-8/MAXIM + CRLF tail, and the AES-CBC (IV=key) crypto.
upstream_docs.title: Fusseldieb/ttlock-reverse-engineering

enter_pairing_mode.notes: Two conditions: the lock must be in setting (factory) mode, and it must be awake. A lock sleeps between uses and is discoverable only for roughly 10-15 seconds after it is woken, so a client should be scanning already, or wake the lock a few seconds after starting its scan — a lock woken too early can fall asleep again before the initialisation finishes.

procedures.basis: kind3r/ttlock-sdk-js (GPL-3.0), whose README documents the wake requirement and the 10-15 second window for its init example.
procedures.name: Touch the keypad to wake a factory-state lock, then initialise

steps.action: If the lock has been added before, factory-reset it first (see setup.factory_reset).
Touch the keypad to wake the lock.
steps.expect: The keypad lights; the lock advertises with its setting-mode flag set.

steps.action: Connect within the window and run the initialisation exchange.

exclusivity.notes: Initialisation only works while the lock is in setting mode, which it advertises as a flag in its advertisement data and leaves for good once an admin is added. Other people get access as eKeys and passcodes the admin issues (through the vendor cloud, in the stock app), not by pairing again.
exclusivity.recovery: A lock that is already initialised will not accept a new admin. Get the current admin to delete the lock from their app (which resets it over BLE), or factory-reset it at the hardware, then initialise it again. Close the TTLock app on nearby phones while doing so.

pairing.notes: Authentication is a custom multi-packet exchange rather than BLE bonding, so nothing appears in the operating system's Bluetooth settings. Initialising a factory-state lock fetches an AES key the lock itself generates and registers the client as admin with credentials the client chooses; every later command is encrypted with that key. No cloud is needed for this: ttlock-sdk-js (the basis of a Home Assistant add-on) initialises, locks and unlocks V3-protocol locks entirely over BLE, though its author reports initialisation sometimes fails and has to be repeated. Treat that add-on (kind3r/hass-addons) as historical evidence, not a maintained base: its README says the author cannot maintain it, citing differently-behaving TTLock variants and unstable BLE, and its last commit is 2022-07-26. The maintained roquerodrigo/ha-ttlock-ble does not initialise locks; it consumes keys from the vendor cloud or from a prior local initialisation. The vendor cloud matters only in the stock app's world, where it stores the lock data after pairing and issues eKeys and passcodes to other users. Possession of the lock is the authorisation — whoever initialises it first owns it — which is why a reset lock should not be left on a door. The key is per-lock and belongs to its owner, so no value appears here.

unpair.notes: Removing the admin is a reset: the stock app's delete sends the lock's reset command over BLE, and ttlock-sdk-js's reset does the same — the lock returns to setting mode with its AES key, admin, passcodes and fingerprints gone. Revoking a non-admin eKey is a cloud-side operation in the vendor's account system rather than anything a local client can do on the lock.

security_advisory.detail: nv1t's teardown of a TTLock-family lock reported a certificate-pinning bypass via a hardcoded string, SQL injection in a lock-info endpoint, and an IDOR / user-enumeration flaw exposing ~502,000 user records with lock passcodes returned by the API — enough to open affected locks. This is a cloud-side issue (not a BLE replay), and its patch status is not established here. Older/plaintext BLE protocol variants are also weakly protected per the RE work.
security_advisory.summary: TTLock's cloud API has had severe public flaws (user enumeration, exposed passcodes) that let a researcher open locks; older BLE variants are weakly protected.

issued_to_client: The per-lock AES key (after successful pairing)
The numeric unlock key, needed for lock/unlock
The numeric admin passcode (admin key holders only), needed for passcode/fingerprint/card management and settings
credentials.notes: The per-lock AES key gates control; it is provisioned at pairing (not a global constant). Lock/unlock also needs the unlock key, and admin operations the admin passcode (ha-ttlock-ble's manual-key form, reported). All three are live per-lock secrets: keep them out of logs, diagnostics and examples. There is no Wi-Fi on the lock itself (a separate TTLock Wi-Fi gateway exists). See the security_advisory: the cloud that issues keys/passcodes has had severe public flaws.
stored_on_device: Per-lock AES key (aesKeyArray), provisioned at pairing

factory_reset.description: The TTLock/Sciener platform is sold under dozens of OEM names and the control layout differs between them, so identify which of these two shapes the lock in hand has before starting. What does not vary is the consequence: a reset lock is wide open on a documented default passcode until it is re-enrolled, so do not reset a door and then walk away from it.
factory_reset.effect: Returns the lock to factory state: the account binding and the per-lock AES key are cleared, along with enrolled passcodes and fingerprints, and the lock reverts to its default master passcode. Any client holding the old key stops working and the lock must be added to an account again to issue a new one.

applies_to: TTLock A260 and similar keypad/fingerprint rebrands
procedures.basis: The TTLock A260 WiFi smart lock user manual, which documents the button, the hold time and the resulting default passcode.
procedures.indicator: Two audible tips from the lock.
procedures.name: Reset button on the rear panel held for five seconds

steps.action: Open the door and find the single Reset button on the back of the rear panel.
Press and hold it for five seconds, until the lock gives two audible tips.
steps.expect: The lock is in factory state and opens to any passcode or fingerprint until it is re-enrolled. The documented default master passcode is 123456 — a product-wide vendor default, not a per-unit secret, and the reason a freshly reset lock should not be left on a door.

steps.action: Press the reset button for three seconds and enter 000# to initialise, if the model prompts for an initialisation passcode.
steps.notes: Documented for the A260; not all rebrands ask for this step.

procedures.basis: The Lagute/Sciener smart lock instructions, which document the setting-button flow used by the models with no keypad.
procedures.indicator: A single beep confirms the lock is empty.
procedures.name: Clear the lock data from the setting button (button-and-beep models)

steps.action: Hold the setting button beside the batteries until a long beep says the lock is in setting mode, and keep holding.
Still in setting mode, hold the unlock button until a beep sounds.
steps.expect: One beep — the lock's data is cleared.

methods.description: Pair with the lock to obtain its per-lock AES key (aesKeyArray), then connect, subscribe to notify char 0000fff4, and write 7F 5A-framed, AES-CBC-encrypted commands to 0000fff2.

steps.action: Pair the lock (via the TTLock app or a client that implements the key exchange) to obtain the per-lock AES key.
Connect, subscribe to 0000fff4, and write framed/encrypted commands to 0000fff2.

setup.notes: Pairing is done through the TTLock app, which registers the lock to a cloud account and provisions the per-lock AES key material; passcodes/eKeys are issued through the cloud but can be used offline. A third-party client needs the lock's aesKeyArray and unlock key (from a successful pairing; plus the admin passcode for admin operations) to drive it locally. A lock that was initialised locally can be driven with those values alone and no TTLock account (ha-ttlock-ble's manual-key path, reported); that path accepts the output of an initialisation, it does not perform one.

rejoin.notes: No network membership; a client with the key re-connects independently.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. The GATT UUIDs, frame layout (magic 7F 5A, CRC-8/MAXIM, CRLF), and AES-CBC/PKCS5 crypto are from Fusseldieb/ttlock-reverse-engineering; the cloud-side vulnerabilities from nv1t's teardown. The Fusseldieb RE authors report their AES key-exchange is not fully solved (residual padding errors), but two open-source implementations report working local control: kind3r/ttlock-sdk-js (init/lock/unlock of V3 locks) and roquerodrigo/ha-ttlock-ble (lock/unlock, state, battery and push events from provisioned keys). Those are third-party success reports, not runs by this project.

artifacts.description: Community RE: GATT UUIDs and gatttool dump, the 7F 5A frame, CRC-8/MAXIM + CRLF tail, AES-CBC (IV = key) crypto. Its authors report the key exchange is not fully solved.
Official closed-core SDK demo: confirms lock, gateway and DFU client APIs exist; publishes no wire format and no firmware image.

Source review 2026-11-11 (custom_components/ttlock_ble/manual_key.py, config_flow.py, advertisement.py, README). Established in code: the cloud-vs-manual setup choice, the manual-key credential set (MAC, 16-byte AES key, numeric unlock key, optional admin passcode, five frame-header values with V3 defaults 5/3/2/1/1), the advertisement cross-check of protocol type/version/scene, and that admin-only features need the admin passcode. Upstream-reported only: real lock/event/battery behaviour and the coverage of the V3 defaults. No lock was driven and no key entered; the upstream test suite could not be run offline (a Home Assistant transitive dependency was missing).

Legacy local pair/reset, credential-management and lock/unlock add-on built on ttlock-sdk-js. Its README says the author cannot maintain it (TTLock variants behave differently; BLE is unstable). The repository is not archived; "unmaintained" is the README's own statement. Historical evidence only; no pair or reset was run.

Official app, read 2026-11-11 for the firmware path only: update metadata is requested per lock (lock ID plus model, hardware and firmware revisions) and the image is downloaded from the URL returned, so there is no reusable public image link. No update metadata was requested and no DFU command sent. The sha256 is of the XAPK bundle.

dfu_mode.notes: Not observed. A stock legacy bootloader advertises "DfuTarg", and whether it moves address depends on the SDK version, so nothing yet binds a DfuTarg advert back to a TTLock lock.

enter.notes: Not documented on purpose. The stack's buttonless entry (01 04 on the legacy control point) is in firmware-update.md; nothing here says whether this firmware honours it.

image.notes: A stock legacy Nordic bootloader takes unsigned images with a CRC-16 init packet; whether Sciener changed that is not established. Images are served per lock (reported, static analysis of the official app 9.9.260902): its update screen asks the vendor cloud for update metadata keyed by the lock ID plus the lock's model, hardware and firmware revisions, then downloads whatever URL comes back for that lock. No owner-independent public image or image URL has been located -- neither the vendor SDK demo nor either open-source integration ships one -- and a generic "TTLock firmware" file would be unsafe across the platform's many model and hardware revisions.

dfu.notes: Service presence from the community reverse engineering; the vendor's closed SDK also exposes a DFU feature. A replacement client should recognise the service and leave it alone: a failed update on a lock can strand the door.

remaining_unknowns: Account-free initialisation of an arbitrary factory-state lock by a maintained tool: ttlock-sdk-js reports it for V3 locks, but the add-on built on it says it is unmaintained; ha-ttlock-ble only consumes keys from a prior initialisation.
Byte offsets of the advertised state (bolt position, battery, records-pending, protocol header values, MAC); they live in the ttlock-ble SDK, which was not inspected.
Whether manufacturer ID 773 (0x0305) is really protocol type 5 / sub-version 3 in the company-ID slot, and what non-V3 locks advertise there.
Which locks the V3 frame-header defaults (5, 3, 2, 1, 1) do not fit, and what they use instead.
Whether Schlage Breeze locks accept the manual-key path; they are known only as a second TTLock-platform account type.
A safe, generic factory-reset procedure across rebrands; the two procedures above are model-specific and unexecuted.
Certificate pinning in the current official app (not dynamically tested), and whether the cloud flaws in the security advisory are patched.
An owner-independent firmware image: none located (not proven not to exist); lock-side image signing is unknown.

characteristics.name: Status notify
characteristics.notes: Framed responses and status; 16-byte encrypted data packets carry a trailing checksum byte.

services.name: TTLock command service (0x1910)
services.notes: Command channel (GATT service 0x1910; per the Fusseldieb gatttool dump the fff2/fff4 characteristics sit inside service 0x1910, not a 0xFFF0 service). Characteristics resolved by UUID: write 0000fff2 (write-without-response), notify 0000fff4. All packets are [12B header (magic 7F 5A ...)][data][CRC-8/MAXIM][CRLF]; data is AES/CBC/PKCS5 with IV = key. A Nordic legacy DFU service (00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123) is also present for OTA; see its own entry below.

format.name: battery_level
format.notes: The SIG-defined layout; not read back from a lock by this project (reported, not confirmed).

services.name: Battery Service (standard 0x180F)
services.notes: Separate primary service, immediately after 0x1910 in the cited GATT dump; the Battery Level characteristic does not belong to the command service.

services.name: Nordic Legacy DFU Service
services.notes: The firmware-update path, not a control surface: list it read-only and never write to it. Present on the lock per the community reverse engineering (Fusseldieb/ttlock-reverse-engineering); its characteristics and the update procedure are intentionally not documented here (bricking risk). See features[type: firmware_update].
